title: Oracle Java Tutorials - Object-Oriented Programming Concepts
passage_text: Oracle's own introduction to the ideas behind object-oriented programming: what an object is, how a class describes a family of objects, and how inheritance, interfaces and packages fit together. Read it first when the gap is about seeing a problem as objects that bundle data with the behaviour that acts on it, rather than as separate procedures and variables.

title: Oracle Java Tutorials - Classes and Objects
passage_text: The reference lesson for turning a design into code: declaring classes, fields, constructors and methods, creating objects, and using nested classes and enums. Work through it alongside your own assignment code and compare how each of your classes combines its data and its behaviour.

title: Oracle Java Tutorials - Controlling Access to Members of a Class
passage_text: Explains Java's access levels (private, package-private, protected, public) and how they let a class hide its internal representation behind a small public interface. This is the mechanism behind encapsulation: change the private fields and only that class needs to change.

title: Refactoring Guru - Encapsulate Field
passage_text: A short worked refactoring that takes a public field and replaces it with private data plus accessor methods, with before-and-after code. Useful as a concrete drill: find a public field in your own code, encapsulate it, and note which other classes did or did not need to change.

title: Oracle Java Tutorials - Interfaces and Inheritance
passage_text: Covers the two main ways Java shares code between classes: inheritance from a superclass and implementing interfaces, including overriding, hiding, abstract classes and polymorphism. Read it when the gap is about reusing behaviour instead of copying it.

title: Refactoring Guru - Design Patterns catalogue
passage_text: A catalogue of the classic creational, structural and behavioural design patterns, each with the problem it solves, a diagram and code examples in several languages. Start with Strategy, Template Method and Factory Method, which are the patterns most often used to reduce duplicated code in coursework-sized programs.

title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.005 - Software Construction
passage_text: MIT's free undergraduate course on writing correct, understandable, ready-for-change software, with readings on specifications, abstract data types, designing classes and testing. Use the readings on ADTs and specifications when you are designing a program for a realistic problem rather than a toy exercise.

title: Refactoring Guru - Refactoring and code smells
passage_text: Explains what refactoring is, the common code smells that signal a design problem, and the step-by-step techniques for fixing each one. Good for the second pass on a working program: when it runs but the marker's feedback says the design is hard to follow or extend.

title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 - Introduction to Algorithms
passage_text: MIT's free introductory algorithms course: lecture videos, notes and problem sets covering the core data structures, sorting, searching, hashing and graph algorithms, and why efficiency matters. Watch the first two lectures for the big picture of what the subject is trying to achieve before drilling into specific structures.

title: Khan Academy - Algorithms
passage_text: A gentle, free introduction to what an algorithm is and how to reason about one: binary search, asymptotic notation, selection and insertion sort, recursion, merge sort and quicksort, with interactive exercises. A good place to rebuild foundations if the overall purpose of the subject still feels abstract.

title: VisuAlgo - visualising data structures and algorithms
passage_text: Animated, step-by-step visualisations of sorting algorithms, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, binary search trees, heaps and graph algorithms. Use it to see what each structure and algorithm actually does before deciding which one a problem calls for.

title: GeeksforGeeks - Data Structures overview
passage_text: An index of the standard data structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, graphs) with the operations each supports and typical uses. Handy for the identification step: given a problem, which structure gives you the operations you need?

title: Oracle Java Tutorials - Collections
passage_text: Oracle's guide to the Java Collections Framework: List, Set, Map, Queue and Deque, their standard implementations (ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, TreeMap, PriorityQueue) and the algorithms in java.util.Collections. Read it when implementing a structure in Java, and to see how the library versions behave.

title: Princeton Algorithms (Sedgewick and Wayne) - booksite
passage_text: The free companion site to the standard Algorithms textbook, with full Java implementations of every data structure and sorting or searching algorithm, plus explanations and exercises. Compare your own Java implementation against theirs line by line.

title: Big-O Cheat Sheet
passage_text: A one-page table of the time and space complexity of the common data structures and sorting algorithms, best, average and worst case. Use it to justify a choice: when the marker asks why you picked a hash table over a tree, or merge sort over insertion sort, this is the comparison to make.

title: Princeton Algorithms - Analysis of Algorithms
passage_text: The chapter on how to measure and compare algorithms: running-time experiments, mathematical models, order-of-growth classifications and memory use. Read it when you need to argue that one approach is better than another rather than just assert it.

title: Princeton Algorithms - Sorting
passage_text: Complete Java implementations and analysis of elementary sorts, mergesort, quicksort and priority queues, with empirical timing comparisons. A model for the design, implement, then evaluate cycle the SILO asks for.

title: Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH)
passage_text: The OpenJDK tool for measuring Java code performance reliably, avoiding the traps of naive System.nanoTime timing loops (warm-up, JIT, dead-code elimination). Use it when your evaluation needs real performance measurements rather than guesses.

title: The Scrum Guide (official)
passage_text: The definitive, short definition of Scrum from its creators: the roles, events and artifacts, and the reasoning behind them. Read it when planning sprints or writing about how the team managed the project, so the terms you use match what the framework actually says.

title: Atlassian Agile Coach
passage_text: Practical articles on running agile projects with Jira: writing user stories, estimating with story points, planning and reviewing sprints, retrospectives and reading burndown charts. Directly relevant to managing a capstone build and to the evidence in your sprint reports.

title: OWASP Top Ten
passage_text: The industry-standard list of the most critical web application security risks, each with how it happens, how to prevent it and example attack scenarios. Check your capstone design against every item, and cite the ones you addressed in your documentation.

title: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
passage_text: Concise, practitioner-written guides on specific secure-development topics: authentication, session management, input validation, password storage, logging, secrets management and more. Use the relevant sheet as the checklist when implementing that part of your system.

title: The Twelve-Factor App
passage_text: Twelve widely adopted principles for building software that deploys cleanly to modern hosting: config in the environment, explicit dependencies, stateless processes, logs as streams, dev and production parity. A recognised industry baseline to measure a capstone deployment against.

title: Google Developer Documentation Style Guide
passage_text: Google's public style guide for writing about technical work clearly: plain language, active voice, consistent terminology, and how to write for readers who are not experts in your system. Apply it when presenting outcomes to a non-technical client or assessor.

title: University of Edinburgh Reflection Toolkit - Gibbs' Reflective Cycle
passage_text: A clear explanation of Gibbs' six-stage model for reflecting on an experience: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan, with prompts for each stage. Use it to structure retrospectives and any reflection on feedback you received.

title: Write the Docs - Documentation guide
passage_text: A community-maintained guide to software documentation: why it matters, how to structure it, what to include in a README, API docs and maintenance guides, and how to keep docs current. Read it before writing or revising a system maintenance document or user manual.

title: arc42 - software architecture documentation template
passage_text: A free, widely used template for documenting a system's architecture in twelve sections: goals and constraints, context, building blocks, runtime and deployment views, cross-cutting concepts, decisions, risks and glossary. A ready-made professional structure for the technical parts of a capstone report.

title: Diataxis - a framework for technical documentation
passage_text: Explains the four kinds of documentation (tutorials, how-to guides, reference, explanation), what each is for, and why mixing them makes documents hard to use. Use it to decide what belongs in a user manual versus a maintenance document.
